name: GHK-Cu / BPC-157
used_for: Marketed by telemedicine and peptide sellers as a skin and tissue repair pairing. These uses are promotional claims, not approved indications.
summary: GHK-Cu / BPC-157 is a pairing of a copper-binding peptide and a gastric-derived research peptide, sold as a mixed or paired product. No approved product contains it, and no combination-specific human study was found in the sources reviewed. A telemedicine article notes that GHK-Cu is in FDA's category 2 for injectable routes and says online discussions often gloss over route and regulatory status. The detailed information is on the pages for GHK-Cu and BPC-157; formulations vary by seller. The combination's side effects are not separately characterized.

internet_claims.claim: A telemedicine company's article markets the pair as a skin and repair stack and warns that most online discussion glosses over the route of administration and the regulatory status of both peptides.

dose.summary: No combination study was found, so there is no studied combined dose. One educational calculator site describes a community mixing recipe of 10 mg GHK-Cu and 5 mg BPC-157 in one vial, and says this is untested.

items.text: CalcMyPeptide, a peptide calculator site, describes a community-developed mix: reconstitute a 10 mg GHK-Cu vial with 3 to 4 mL of bacteriostatic water instead of the standard 2 mL, then add the contents of a 5 mg BPC-157 vial to the same solution, about a 2 to 1 GHK-Cu to BPC-157 ratio. The page cites no studies.
items.label: internet

timing.summary: No study tested timing for the pair. A three-peptide guide that includes both says they can be injected in the same session.

items.text: PeptideWiki, a guide with affiliate links to peptide sellers, covers a three-peptide stack of GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500 and says all three can be injected in the same session using separate syringes.
items.label: internet

storage_and_handling.summary: No stability study of a mixed GHK-Cu and BPC-157 product was found. Online sources disagree on whether the two can share a vial or syringe.

items.text: PeptIQ, a peptide app and education site, says GHK-Cu is compatible with a BPC-157 plus TB-500 draw in one syringe, but also says never to add bacteriostatic water to multiple peptides in the same vial, and to draw immediately before injecting rather than pre-drawing syringes.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptideWiki, with affiliate links to peptide sellers, says of its GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500 stack not to mix the peptides in the same syringe because stability and compatibility data for combined solutions is limited.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with supplier and affiliate links, says of the GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500 stack not to combine them in one syringe because their stability and pH profiles differ, and to use a separate syringe for each.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Online reports
side_effect_groups.summary: No combination safety data exists. One educational site reports, without any study, that mixing the two in one vial reduces injection pain.

items.text: CalcMyPeptide says GHK-Cu alone causes burning injection pain because its solution is acidic (pH about 3.5 to 4.5), and that the community mix of both peptides in one vial with extra water reduces pain from severe burning (8 to 9 out of 10) to a mild sting (2 to 3 out of 10). The page cites no studies.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Warnings
side_effect_groups.summary: A telemedicine seller notes that online discussion often skips route of administration and regulatory status for both peptides.
